title: Argentina condemns Princess Anne’s visit to Malvinas

 Argentina condemns Princess Anne’s visit to Malvinas
 Government describes the British royal’s official engagements on UK-administered territory as a "provocation" amid growing tensions over oil exploration in disputed waters.
 James Grainger 
 Editor-in-Chief, Buenos Aires Times.
 Share this News 
 Princess Anne on the Malvinas (Falkland) Islands. | cedoc/perfil 
 Argentina's government on Tuesday rejected official engagements by Princess Anne at the Malvinas (Falkland) Islands, an archipelago claimed by Buenos Aires, where the two countries are embroiled in a renewed dispute over hydrocarbon exploration.
 The Foreign Ministry in Buenos Aires said the visit by King Charles III’s sister was taking place “in the exercise of the illegal British occupation of the Malvinas Islands, South Georgia, the South Sandwich Islands and the surrounding maritime areas,” in a statement posted on social media.
 The Ministry described the visit as “a provocation,” coming as the United Kingdom pursues what it called the “unilateral illegal exploitation of hydrocarbons through the granting of illegitimate licences” in the South Atlantic.
 In October, President Javier Milei's government asked the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea to intervene to halt the Sea Lion oil project, led by British company Rockhopper and Israeli firm Navitas.

 The move followed an announcement by Rockhopper that it expected to begin extracting hydrocarbons in the North Malvinas Basin around January 2028.
 The tribunal has provisionally set November 28, 2026, as the date for issuing its decision on Buenos Aires’ request for urgent provisional measures, according to its website.
 The project has intensified diplomatic tensions between the two countries, which fought a brief but bloody war in 1982 over control of the islands, then under British administration. The conflict ended with the surrender of Argentina’s military dictatorship.
 Read more...

 London does not recognise Argentina’s claim to the islands, which have been under British control since 1833.
 President Milei had previously called on London to halt the Sea Lion project, describing it as “illegal plundering” of Argentina’s natural resources.
 He has also promoted legislation in Congress, which is still under consideration, to toughen penalties for the exploitation of natural resources in the islands.

 In mid-September, an Argentine court also issued an injunction seeking to halt the project following a legal challenge by two Argentine organisations citing potential environmental damage.
 London maintains that the islanders have the right to develop their natural resources and backs the companies involved.
 For decades, the United Nations (UN) has recognised the sovereignty dispute between the two countries and urged both sides to refrain from taking unilateral decisions concerning the territory.
